title: Maker of heaven and earth
hook: the world is made, meant and good (Genesis 1:31)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was creed: credo, I believe, and three questions at the water. Your line was a token broken in two.

A meal. A birthday card. A shelf that's only slightly crooked. A garden bed. Making something by hand often ends with a small moment: the maker steps back and looks. A breath out. That's good. Not perfect, maybe, but good, and theirs, and meant. The creed's very first sentence says that about everything. After I believe in God the Father Almighty comes: Maker of heaven and earth. And the Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back to look at all of it: light and sea, trees and fish, animals and people. Today's word is that first line of the creed, and the first thing Christians say about the world.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU MADE.` → `STEPPING BACK: THAT'S GOOD.` → `THE CREED'S FIRST CLAIM.`

segments.voice: The Bible opens: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The Hebrew verb for created is bara, and here's the surprise: when it means create, in the Bible, its subject is always God. People make, build, shape. Only God bara. Christians draw three things from this line. First, the world is made. It isn't an accident, and it isn't God. It's distinct from God, the way a song is distinct from the singer. Christian thinkers from the second century on said God made it out of nothing, not from material already lying around. Second, the world is meant. It has a purpose. It's here because someone wanted it to be. Third, the world is good. Six times in Genesis 1, God sees that what was made is good. The seventh time, looking at everything together, people included: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." That mattered in the early church. Some teachers, often called Gnostics, taught that the material world was a mistake or a prison, and the body something to escape. The church said no. Matter, bodies, food, sex, earth, stars: made by God, and good. Christians today read Genesis in different ways alongside science. Some read the six days as literal days. Many churches, Catholic and many Protestant, see no conflict between creation and evolution: Genesis tells who and why, science tells how. They differ on how, but share the same first line. Made. Meant. Very good.
screen: `BARA: ONLY GOD CREATES.` · `MADE, NOT AN ACCIDENT.` · `MEANT, FOR A PURPOSE.` · `GOOD: THE BODY IS NO PRISON.` · then, large: `BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at something near you, a leaf, your own hand, a cup, the sky out the window, the way you'd look at something you'd made yourself: its color, its shape, how it works. Then quietly say: very good. If you pray, thank God, Maker of heaven and earth, for it; if you don't, just let yourself see it as good, and meant.
Bara. The Hebrew verb for create, used in the Bible only with God as its subject: the world made, meant, and very good.
Your line: very good. The seventh look, at everything together. Day two hundred ninety-eight, done.

howItsDone: Christians say "Maker of heaven and earth" in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, give thanks for creation in grace before meals, and many churches keep a Season of Creation each autumn.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): hook no longer opens 'Think of' or tells the listener what they felt; bara claim narrowed to its sense 'create' (the verb has another sense with human subjects); 'many Christian thinkers' softened.
'Six times' God sees that it is good (1:4, 10, 12, 18, 21, 25), and a seventh, 'very good', in 1:31. Confirm the count (some manuscripts/versions differ, e.g. the Septuagint adds 'good' at 1:8).
bara: in the Qal stem the subject is always God; script simplifies to 'only God is ever its subject'. Confirm.
Creation from nothing: articulated from the 2nd century (Theophilus of Antioch, Irenaeus). Script says 'from the second century on'.
Gnostics summarized broadly; scholars debate the category. Confirm fairness.
Readings of Genesis and science given without ranking; Catholic acceptance of evolution (e.g. Humani Generis, John Paul II 1996).
